To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) insulin and epidermal‐growth‐factor (EGF) family receptors have a common ligand‐binding mechanism, in which the ligand closes the LRR‐LRR module, (2) the ligand‐inducible dimerization mechanism of the EGFR family is conserved in the insulin family, (3) the ligand induces a change in the dimer interface in the insulin family and the EGF family, (4) this change is mediated

the insulin receptor (IR) is a preassembled dimer that is activated by insulin by a mechanism that is analogous to that used by the epidermal‐growth‐factor receptor (EGFR), and that the IR and EGFR share a common activation mechanism that involves the “closing” of a conserved ligand binding module.

insulin binds to one leucine‐ rich‐repeat‐like (LRR‐like) domain in the ligand ‐binding module of the insulin receptor (IR) (L1) and that this binding induces a conformational change that allows a second LRR‐like domain (L2) to bind to the same insulin molecule, thus closing the LRR‐like module.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanism of insulin‐receptor signaling, which is of fundamental importance for the development of novel therapies in the treatment of diabetes and cancer.
the molecular mechanisms of signal transduction in the insulin receptor (IR), a key player in the control of cellular metabolism and growth in mammals.
the molecular basis of insulin receptor function and regulation and the role of this receptor in insulin resistance and diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insulin binds the L1‐L2 domain of the IR, and that the L1‐domain binds insulin directly.
the insulin receptor (IR) is a disulfides‐linked (α2β2)4 tetramer that undergoes a ligand‐inducible conformational change to form an (α2β4)4 octameric complex.
the ligand‐bound IR is a dimeric molecule that has a conformation that is different from that of the unliganded receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LRRs in both IR and EGFR are “dual‐function” domains that are required both to bind ligand and to mediate dimerization and activation of the kinase domains.
the ligand‐inducing activation of the insulin receptor is similar to the ligand‐dependent activation of the epidermal receptor.
IR is a dimeric receptor, but that ligand binding to the L1‐L2 module induces a transition that breaks autoinhibitors and remodels the dimer to activate it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ligand‐inducible “closing” of the L1‐L2 module is the common mechanism of activation for all IR and EGFR members.
the ligand‐inducing activation mechanism of EGFR is not unique, but rather is a shared mechanism of RTKs that use a ligand‐binding domain composed of two LRRs connected by a CR domain.
the IR and EGFR ligand‐binding modules have evolved similar activation mechanisms, despite their unique extracellular domains.
